title: VH-1: MTV for Your Parents
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of VH1 from its 1985 launch as a mellower, adult-contemporary sibling to MTV, through its near-collapse in the mid-1990s, John Sykes' turnaround, hits like Pop Up Video, Storytellers, Legends and Behind the Music, the Divas concerts, the shift to countdowns and pop-culture shows like I Love the '80s and Best Week Ever, and its move into celebreality (Surviving Nugent, Flavor of Love, Celebrity Rehab) and the 2009 Ryan Jenkins scandal. They close with listener mail about Chuckstradamus predictions.
topics: Ryan Jenkins murder of Jasmine Fiore

segments.title: Opening banter and VH1's origins
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about music videos and a concert, then introduce VH1's 1985 launch as an older, mellower MTV sibling created to compete with Ted Turner's music channel, and its early VJs and music lineup.

segments.title: Early VJs and lineup
segments.summary: Discussion of the early VH1 VJs, former radio hosts such as Don Imus and Frankie Crocker, Scott Shannon's Morning Zoo format, and the channel's early willingness to show black artists.

segments.title: Comedy on VH1
segments.summary: Rosie O'Donnell started as a VJ on VH1, and Stand Up Spotlight aired, offering stand-up before Comedy Channel launched; MTV had its Half Hour Comedy Hour.

segments.title: Early originals, promo videos and the mid-1990s slump
segments.summary: Peter Noone hosted a trivia-based DJ show; the channel relied on older promotional clips since many acts' prime predated music videos. In the mid-1990s VH1 lacked identity and cable operators tried to drop it.

segments.title: John Sykes turnaround
segments.summary: John Sykes was hired in 1994 and revitalized VH1; subscriber base grew from 49 million to 62 million households in three years, the so-called Sykes effect.

segments.title: Pop Up Video
segments.summary: Pop Up Video, created by Woody Thompson and Ted Lowe, added pop-up trivia bubbles to music videos and became a hit thanks to good writing.

segments.title: Storytellers, Legends and Behind the Music
segments.summary: Storytellers (1996) featured classic rock artists in intimate settings; Legends (1996) offered documentaries; Behind the Music (1997) became known for melodrama, including the Leif Garrett episode, and ran until 2014.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Fashion Awards, Save the Music and Clinton
segments.summary: VH1 partnered with Vogue for the Fashion Awards, where Derek Zoolander appeared; Save the Music launched in 1997 with John Sykes as principal for a day; Bill Clinton donated a saxophone and got a documentary.

segments.title: Divas concerts and I Want My VH1 protest
segments.summary: The Divas concert series began in 1998 with artists including Aretha Franklin, Mariah Carey and Celine Dion. Cable dropping prompted a Denver protest with Don Henley, John Mellencamp and Jewel, after which the operator restored the channel.

segments.title: Dad rock and channel rebranding
segments.summary: Hosts discuss dad rock and Wilco, concert start times, and VH1's many spin-off channel names such as VH1 Soul, VH1 Smooth, and VH1 Classic, which became MTV Classic.

segments.title: Shift to countdowns and Greatest Countdowns
segments.summary: Video airplay dropped sharply; VH1 moved to countdown shows, starting with a Kevin Bacon-hosted 100 Greatest Artists of Rock and Roll, followed by a Greatest countdown franchise running until 2012.

segments.title: Where Are They Now and VH1 movies
segments.summary: Where Are They Now (1999) followed one-hit wonders and former child stars; VH1 made the film Two of Us (2000) about a fictional Lennon and McCartney night.

segments.title: Jeff Olde, agile management and I Love the 80s
segments.summary: Brian Graden hired Jeff Olde, who gave producers free rein under an agile management approach; cheap pop culture shows such as I Love the 80s (2002) became hits, leading to Talk Soup-style clip shows and Best Week Ever.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Celebreality and Surviving Nugent
segments.summary: VH1 coined the term celebreality; Ted Nugent's Surviving Nugent was an early example. Surreal Life led to Flavor of Love, Strange Love, I Love New York, Rock of Love, My Fair Brady, and others.

segments.title: Black audiences and Celebrity Rehab
segments.summary: VH1 became a leading network in African American households in 2014 and drew criticism for stereotypes. Celebrity Rehab with Drew Pinsky (2008) drew criticism over patient deaths.

segments.title: Trans representation, Ryan Jenkins scandal and later shows
segments.summary: VH1 shows with Laverne Cox and Transform Me; 2009 Ryan Jenkins murder of Jasmine Fiore, linked to Fifty One Minds shows, prompted VH1 to distance itself. Later shows included RuPaul's Drag Race, Love and Hip Hop, Basketball Wives and Wild 'N Out.

segments.title: Listener mail: Chuckstradamus
segments.summary: A listener, Brenda from Dallas, writes that Chuck predicted the Smoke TV show about arsonist John Leonard, and Chuck allows it as a Chuckstradamus prediction.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, invite email, and close the episode.
